title: India's Inbound Tourism Problem: Overseas Marketing Budget Slashed to ₹3.5 Crore
excerpt: India's overseas tourism promotion allocation has collapsed from ₹542 crore in 2019 to ₹3.5 crore in FY27, leaving the country's inbound recovery lagging behind competitors while outbound travel booms.
body:
• India's overseas tourism promotion budget dropped to ₹3.5 crore ($420,000) for FY27 — down from ₹542 crore in 2019
  • Foreign tourist arrivals remain at 81% of pre-pandemic levels as of mid-2025, while outbound travel surges
  • The overall tourism ministry budget fell 4% to ₹2,438 crore for FY27, with only 33% of FY26's PRASHAD and Swadesh Darshan allocation actually spent
  • Industry bodies have called the budget a blow to inbound tourism, while the 2% TCS reduction benefits outbound operators

A Marketing Budget Smaller Than Most Hotels'

India allocated just ₹3.5 crore (approximately $420,000) for overseas tourism promotion in the FY2026-27 budget — a figure so small that industry leaders have compared it unfavourably to a single hotel chain's marketing spend, according to a LinkedIn analysis by Prateek Hira, an inbound tourism operator.

The number represents a staggering decline from ₹542 crore allocated for overseas promotion in 2019, as reported by Crisil Intelligence's Pushan Sharma. The collapse has left India's international visibility far behind competitors like Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines, Georgia, and Azerbaijan, all of which maintain robust global tourism marketing campaigns.

"The removal of meaningful allocations for global tourism marketing has dealt a severe blow to inbound tourism. The export component of Indian tourism has been left to fend for itself."

— Rajeev Kohli, Joint Managing Director, Creative Travel

Recovery That Never Arrived

The marketing drought has real consequences. Foreign tourist arrivals stood at only 81% of pre-pandemic levels as of the first nine months of 2025, according to Crisil data cited by Travel Biz Monitor. Meanwhile, Indian outbound travel has surged past pre-pandemic numbers, creating an asymmetry that concerns the industry.

The Union Budget 2026 did reduce the Tax Collected at Source (TCS) on outbound tour packages to a flat 2%, easing cash-flow pressures for outbound operators. But inbound operators received no comparable relief.

The total tourism ministry allocation for FY27 fell 4% to ₹2,438 crore, with the bulk directed toward infrastructure schemes like Swadesh Darshan (₹1,905 crore) and PRASHAD. However, the FY26 Swadesh Darshan scheme had utilised only ₹517 crore of its ₹1,900 crore outlay — a 27% utilisation rate — according to budget documents reviewed by Mint.

Infrastructure Without Promotion

The budget did include substantive infrastructure proposals: high-speed rail corridors, seaplane manufacturing incentives, medical tourism hubs, and the development of 15 archaeological sites including Lothal, Dholavira, and Sarnath.

Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman proposed training 10,000 guides across 20 top tourist destinations, establishing a National Institute of Hospitality, and creating trekking trails in the Himalayas and Western Ghats. A Buddhist circuit in northeastern states was also proposed.

"We were expecting a clear Budgetary allocation for international tourism promotion, which appears to have been missed. Strengthening India's visibility in global markets is critical to accelerating inbound tourism."

— Rajiv Mehra, General Secretary, Federation of Associations in Indian Tourism and Hospitality

Travel Trade Journal noted that while the budget reframed tourism as an employment and infrastructure priority, the persistent absence of a global branding push remained a concern for operators focused on foreign arrivals.

What the Diaspora Sees

For the Indian diaspora abroad, the marketing gap is personal. Many NRIs actively promote India as a travel destination to friends and colleagues, but find that the country lacks the institutional marketing presence that competing destinations deploy in Western markets. Without sustained campaigns in key source markets like the United States, United Kingdom, and Europe, India risks losing ground in the $1.8 trillion global tourism market even as its domestic tourism infrastructure improves.
